slides.say: How many different arrangements of all the letters of the word banana are there? An arrangement does not have to be a real word.
So we arrange six letters, B, A, N, A, N, A. Some letters repeat. A appears three times, and N twice.

We'll solve it in two different ways. Let's start with the math way, like the A A A B example in the lesson. First we count as if all six letters were different. Six factorial is seven hundred twenty.
at: Six factorial is seven hundred twenty

slides.say: But A appears three times. Swapping the As gives nothing new, so we divide by three factorial, six.
And N appears twice. Swapping the Ns gives nothing new either, so we divide by two factorial, two.
Six times two is twelve. Then seven hundred twenty divided by twelve is sixty.
at: seven hundred twenty divided by twelve

slides.say: The traps forget one of the repeats. Dividing only by six gives a hundred twenty, choice number two. Dividing only by two gives three hundred sixty, choice number four.
[pause] Now another way. We have six places, and we choose where each letter goes.
First the three As. We choose three places out of six. That's a group, so six times five times four, divided by three factorial. A hundred twenty divided by six is twenty.
at: We choose three places out of six

slides.say: Three places are left. The two Ns take two of them. Choosing two of three is the same as choosing the one that stays out, three ways.
And B takes the last place. One way.
Twenty times three times one is sixty again.
Choice number three is our answer, and I'll see you in the next question.
at: Choice number three is our answer
